label: Proposition A
title: Charter Changes Affecting Various City Departments and Commissions
q: Shall the City amend the Charter to align it with how some City departments currently operate, change some processes, eliminate or reorganize certain commissions and advisory bodies, and require the Board of Supervisors to amend voter-approved laws to enact some of these changes?
now: The Charter is the City's constitution. It and other voter-passed laws create many commissions and advisory bodies and set their duties, members and reports, and most of it can change only by a public vote. A task force created by 2024's Prop E counted 152 City bodies, 115 of them active, and reported in January 2026.${FS([1, 24])}
does: Rewrites 79 Charter sections to match how departments work now, ends the Public Works and Sanitation and Streets commissions, moves 12 sections into City code, lets legal settlements pass by resolution, sets a commission review every ten years from 2035, and requires or allows the Board to change some voter-passed ordinances, including ending the Our City Our Home Oversight Committee.${FS([1, 22, 9, 10, 16, 12])}
yes: You want these Charter changes, including ending two commissions and letting the Board change some voter-created bodies and laws by ordinance.${F(1)}
no: You want to keep the Charter as it is. The current task force would expire January 31, 2027, and bodies voters created would still need a vote to change.${FS([1, 11])}

y1.s: Supporters say the Charter still carries bodies that serve no purpose, like a commission over a department that no longer exists, and only voters can remove them.
g: After decades the charter can end up with zombie commissions that serve no purpose.
the Sanitation and Streets Commission oversees a non-existent department
The charter has become an accumulation of commissions, reporting requirements and procedural rules for a San Francisco that no longer exists.
only ones that are idle or redundant.
has too many commissions and committees that create bottlenecks and unnecessary hearings.
San Francisco has accumulated numerous overlapping, inactive or duplicative bodies that can diffuse responsibility and consume staff resources.
reduced the efficiency of City government and made it less responsive to current needs.
many of them duplicate existing city functions
src: "For example, the Sanitation and Streets Commission oversees a department that doesn't exist, and the charter still references a Parking Authority that voters removed a decade ago."
"Because Charter amendments require costly political campaigns, many Charter bodies remain outdated as the City changes"
y1.fig: The department claim checks out, but both commissions Prop A ends were still meeting. Public Works took over the Department of Sanitation and Streets' duties on January 1, 2023, and the Sanitation and Streets Commission kept setting standards for Public Works: it met 9 times in 2023, 8 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. The Public Works Commission met 9 times in 2022, 23 in 2023, 17 in 2024, 17 in 2025 and 11 in 2026 through September 24. The task force counted 152 City bodies, 115 of them active; 42 were created by the Charter alone and 13 by both the Charter and code. The proponents' "60 advisory bodies and commissions" could not be reproduced from the sponsor's crosswalk or the task force report. Unverified.
resp: "there is a real difference between eliminating an inactive body and weakening an active one"

y2.s: Supporters say small updates to bodies voters created, like how often they meet or who may sit on them, shouldn't wait for a citywide election.
g: Prop A lets the Board handle those small fixes through ordinary legislation instead.
would let elected policymakers change them as needs and priorities change.
in light of experience and current needs and priorities.
moves some of them under the Administrative Code (where they can be adjusted by the BOS without a ballot measure)
src: "But right now, even small administrative updates to some of these commissions — like adjusting how often they meet, or the qualifications of their members — have to go before voters as a ballot measure."
"THE ADMINISTRATIVE CODE EXISTS FOR A REASON AND PROVISIONS THAT LIVE THERE CAN BE UPDATED TO THE NORMAL LEGISLATIVE PROCESS AS CONDITIONS CHANGE"
y2.fig: The record shows voter-only rules can sit unfixed for years. The state labor board declared the Charter's strike-discipline section "void and unenforceable" in 2023, and it is still in the Charter because only voters can remove it. On January 1, 2027, Prop A moves 12 Charter sections into City code, where a Board majority of 6 of 11 can amend them, subject to the Mayor's veto. Bodies it moves include the Human Services and Disability and Aging Services commissions and the SFMTA and PUC citizens' advisory councils; the SFMTA council can then be changed by resolution of the SFMTA board. The rebuttal's "hundreds of thousands of dollars in campaign costs" has no source; the 2024 measure that created the task force was backed by $117,000, per Mission Local. Unverified.
resp: "The charter should be improved, but not at the expense of transparency, and checks on government power."

y3.s: Supporters say duplicate reporting and needless commissions waste staff time, and the Controller puts the saving at $365,000 to $450,000 a year.
g: forcing employees into busy work that wastes time and money.
City Hall has too much bureaucracy that slows everything down.
will reduce redundant bureaucracy and create a more efficient and responsive government.
src: "it would have a moderate impact on the cost of government, saving $365,000 to $450,000 annually."
"The Sanitation and Streets Commission and Public Works Commission shared two full-time staff members with annual costs of $336,000."
y3.fig: The saving is real but small against the budget, and the department's own estimate was smaller still. The Controller's $365,000 to $450,000 a year comes from ending three bodies, and $336,000 of it is two shared staff. That is 0.0022% to 0.0027% of the $16.85 billion FY2026-27 budget, 1.08% to 1.33% of the $33,894,772 a year the Budget and Legislative Analyst counted for 111 bodies, and 37.1% to 45.8% of the $983,528 the three bodies cost. For that analyst, the department estimated $73,536 saved by ending the Sanitation and Streets Commission, which costs $251,839, and gave no estimate ("n.a.") for ending the Public Works Commission, which costs $715,570. The task force said staff supported 1,560 meetings in FY2024, and the Civil Grand Jury estimated commission work takes about 8% of senior department staff time. Prop A adds costs too: the next task force (the 2025 one took about 5,900 staff hours) and possibly $5,000 to $85,000 a year to pay Youth Commission members. The proponents don't name the duplicate reports Prop A removes, and none was identified. Unverified.
resp: "SAN FRANCISCANS PASSED PROPOSITION E IN NOVEMBER OF 2024 TO REDUCE DUPLICATION AND INCREASE THE EFFICIENCY OF OUR BOARDS, COMMISSIONS AND ADVISORY BOARDS NOT TO CONCENTRATE EVEN MORE POWER IN THE HANDS OF THE MAYOR'S OFFICE"

y4.s: Supporters say Prop A clears out rules overtaken by technology or court rulings, like a required bookbinder and a strike ban the state labor board voided.
g: the current system still requires the city to employ a bookbinder
trim outdated bureaucratic language and modernizing operations to create a charter that offers greater accountability
nearly all are technical, administrative, or housekeeping changes
Requiring a citywide election to fix a typo or fix outdated language isn't democracy
src: "New technology can make old laws pointless. For example, the current system still requires the city to employ a bookbinder and to publish laws in daily print editions of the Chronicle that no longer exist."
"Lawmakers sometimes make typos and mistakes when writing legislation, leaving behind laws that are confusing or just don't make sense. Prop A cleans up some of the worst examples."
y4.fig: The examples match the text, though some matter only on paper. The Law Library section names a "Bookbinder", and payroll data show no bookbinder on the Law Library payroll in any year from FY2012-13 to FY2025-26. The state labor board held the strike-discipline section "void and unenforceable" in 2023, and Prop A deletes it. Prop A strikes references to a Parking Authority in retiree health sections. It does not itself change the official newspaper rule; it lets the Board amend that ordinance by a two-thirds vote, as long as it keeps a way to support local news. Section 1 lists 79 Charter sections revised and 14 deleted; the sponsor's crosswalk has 115 rows.
resp: "it usually means people are trying to hide something in the fine print"

y5.s: Supporters say removing commissions that sit between departments and elected officials makes it clear who answers for results.
g: Departments will answer to elected individuals, not unelected commissioners
favored clearer lines of accountability and a more streamlined government structure
it just makes City Hall less accountable for delivering results for voters.
src: "WE ARE GETTING RID OF A FEW COMMISSIONS. THE STREETS AND SANITATION COMMISSION, THE PUBLIC WORKS COMMISSION WE CONSULTED WITH INTERESTED STAKEHOLDERS THERE AND EVERYONE SORT OF FELT LIKE YEAH, THOSE COMMISSIONS COULD PROBABLY GO."
"the long-standing existing protest process provides losing bidders adequate recourse"
y5.fig: Without its two commissions, Public Works answers to the Mayor directly. Contracts above the City threshold would be approved by the Mayor and awarded by the Director under Administrative Code §6.3, instead of voted on at a public commission meeting. The budget hearing becomes a department-run public meeting under Administrative Code §3.3(b)(2), with 72 hours' notice but outside the Brown Act and Sunshine Ordinance. The Board's own budget hearings continue. Our reading of Charter §10.104, not confirmed by any official source: the Public Works Director would serve at the Mayor's pleasure. Unverified.
resp: "stripping citizen oversight and consolidating even more executive branch power"

y6.s: Supporters say none of the bodies overseeing homeless services is removed; Prop A only lets the Board adjust them without an election.
g: Currently five separate, overlapping commissions oversee homeless services in San Francisco. None of them are removed by Prop A.
will not be eliminated by Prop A
one of several advisory bodies with jurisdiction over this broad service area
src: "Currently five separate, overlapping commissions oversee homeless services in San Francisco. None of them are removed by Prop A."
"Makes no changes to body at this moment, but gives the board the ability to amend via ordinance in the future"
y6.fig: Prop A ends none of the homelessness bodies, but it lets the City end one, the Our City Our Home Oversight Committee, by ordinance. The task force counted five bodies advising on homelessness in late 2025, and it voted unanimously on October 15, 2025 to eliminate the Our City Our Home committee; Prop A turned that into an option with no deadline. The Shelter Monitoring Committee was eliminated effective June 29, 2026, before the arguments were written. The proponents don't name their five bodies, and which action ended the Shelter Monitoring Committee wasn't identified. Unverified. The Homelessness Oversight Commission keeps its seven seats, with two reserved for people who have experienced homelessness.
resp: "The measure allows the Board of Supervisors to remove independent oversight with a majority vote."

y7.s: Supporters say a task force every ten years keeps the system current, and this measure is a first step the City can build on.
g: This is step one towards reducing SF's government bureaucracy
making future reforms easier to implement.
requires regular convening of a Commission Streamlining Task Force every 10-years to review the commission system
src: "require a task force to meet every ten years to recommend changes to commissions."
"By no earlier than January 1, 2035, and no later than February 1, 2035, and at ten year intervals following those dates, a Commission Streamlining Task Force ... shall be convened"
y7.fig: The next task force starts in 2035, with five seats: the City Administrator, Controller and City Attorney or their staff, a public-sector labor member chosen by the Board President, and an open-government expert chosen by the Mayor. Its ordinances on bodies created by ordinance take effect in 90 days unless two-thirds of the Board vote them down, as the current task force's do; bodies only voters can change are excluded. Prop A drops the Budget and Legislative Analyst's cost report and the City Attorney's draft Charter amendment from the process. The current task force ends January 1, 2027, instead of January 31, 2027. The 2025 task force took about 5,900 staff hours.
resp: "makes it easier in the future to further reduce City Hall's transparency."

y8.s: Supporters say the package came from departments and a months-long public process, and keeps only the task force ideas most people agree on.
g: VOTE YES ON PROP A THE CITYWIDE GOOD GOVERNMENT CONSENSUS MEASURE
were meant to be non-controversial improvements
those substantive, controversial recommendations are not in Prop A.
While the final package avoids more controversial but needed reforms
The task force wanted bigger cuts. Supervisors flinched.
far more modest than they suggest
src: "Department heads, commissions, and the public suggest changes through a transparent, months-long process. The mayor and a supermajority of the Board of Supervisors agreed on 110 small fixes that will help city government serve you better."
"On July 14, 2026, the Board of Supervisors voted 9 to 2 to place Proposition A on the ballot."
y8.fig: The Board vote was 9 to 2, and the measure carries a narrower part of the task force's plan. It was introduced May 19, 2026, amended in Rules Committee June 22 and placed on July 14; Supervisors Chan and Fielder voted no. The sponsor described "APPROXIMATELY 110" changes, and his crosswalk lists 115. No affected body voted on Prop A in any minutes posted through October 2026. SPUR says the task force recommended cutting Charter bodies from 42 to 24, and GrowSF says Prop A takes them from 55 to 38. Unverified.
resp: "None of the five changes listed above were discussed, or voted on, by the Commission Streamlining Task Force."

n1.s: Opponents say moving voter-created bodies into code lets a simple Board majority change or end what voters put in place.
g: There are grievous mistakes in Prop A that threaten participatory democracy by removing commissions put in place by voters.
Commissions don't land in the Charter by accident.
effectively allowing the removal of commissions put in place by voters.
could later change or eliminate voter-created oversight bodies with a simple vote.
would allow the supes to overturn existing voter-approved legislation
attempting to take away our voices from participating in direct democracy
combines many consequential changes in a single measure and would weaken or make it easier to change several channels for public oversight.
"Prop. A" dismantles wholesale, citizen-involved democracy in San Francisco!
src: "OR TO STRIP VOTERS OF THE POWER TO MAKE FUTURE CHANGES."
"to enable these sections to be amended or deleted in the future consistent with the process for amending and deleting other Board of Supervisors-adopted provisions"
n1.fig: The measure takes voter-only protection from 12 Charter sections and from one voter-passed committee, and requires six named changes to voter-passed ordinances by July 31, 2027. The 12 sections, including the Human Services and Disability and Aging Services commissions, move into code on January 1, 2027, where 6 of 11 supervisors can amend them, subject to the Mayor's veto. The Police, Police Accountability, Elections and Ethics bodies stay in the Charter. New §14.101.1 adds its powers "in addition to any other amendments authorized by Section 14.101", so it does not change how other initiative ordinances are protected. Open question: does the Board's new power over voter-passed ordinances stay limited to the changes Prop A names, and can text the Board writes under it be changed again without a vote? The text is silent and no City Attorney opinion was found.
resp: "Requiring a citywide election to fix a typo or fix outdated language isn't democracy, it just makes City Hall less accountable for delivering results for voters."

n2.s: Opponents say Prop A targets the committee that watches over the Our City, Our Home homelessness fund, which a Board majority could then abolish.
g: Prop A attempts to silence the voices of homeless people and their allies that challenge power, and this particular body was targeted only because of its effectiveness in doing so.
Prop A specifically targets the Our City, Our Home Oversight Committee.
Prop A could threaten the independence of bodies important to DSA SF, including the Our City Our Home commission
eliminate the our city our home oversight board
src: "Take independent oversight for November 2018 Proposition C. The measure allows the Board of Supervisors to remove independent oversight with a majority vote."
"to amend or eliminate any aspect of the Our City Our Home Oversight Committee"
n2.fig: The committee oversees a fund that spent about $1.2 billion from FY21 to FY25, about 30% of the homelessness department's budget, and costs $310,141 a year to run. Prop A lets the City change or end the committee by ordinance; it does not touch the tax or the fund's legal limits on spending. On the trend the Coalition cites, there are two different counts: people in tents, structures or on the street fell 13% from 2022 to 2024 (3,347 to 2,912), while all unsheltered people, including those in vehicles, fell 1%. The 2026 preliminary count puts all unsheltered people at 3,400, down from 4,354 in 2024, and all homeless people at 7,973, down from 8,323. Neither count shows what caused the change. The argument's 8,400 people housed and 2,800 children have no source; the Coalition's 2025 letter to the task force said 5,000 and 1,700. Portland's 67% is a 2025 Multnomah County count after a change in method, and San Diego's 2024 regional rise was 3%, not 26%. Unverified.
resp: "Currently five separate, overlapping commissions oversee homeless services in San Francisco. None of them are removed by Prop A."

n3.s: Opponents say Prop A moves power from commissions and the Board toward the Mayor, alongside the Mayor's own Charter measures D, E and F.
g: take power away from the public and give it to the mayor
This is an unnecessary expansion of mayoral power
a transfer of power to the Mayor's office
it strips too much power from the people and hands it to City Hall
to increase the power of the mayor's office and eliminate community oversight of city hall
Reject the power grab. No SF Kings.
src: "NOT TO CONCENTRATE EVEN MORE POWER IN THE HANDS OF THE MAYOR'S OFFICE TO TAKE A HATCHET TO COMMISSIONS THAT PROVIDE OVERSIGHT AND TRANSPARENCY FOR THE PUBLIC"
"shall be appointed by the Mayor under Section 3.100(18)"
n3.fig: The shift is concrete in three places. The Mayor's four Homelessness Oversight Commission appointees would take office unless 8 of 11 supervisors reject them within 30 days, where today the Board must approve them after a hearing within 60 days. With its commissions gone, Public Works contracts above the City threshold go to the Mayor for approval and the Director for award, and the budget hearing becomes a department meeting. Prop A's rules for reading measures together name D, E and F: if A and E both pass, the City Administrator gains authority over City real estate, and F prevails over A on removal rules. Our reading of Charter §10.104, not confirmed by any official source: the Public Works Director would serve at the Mayor's pleasure. Unverified. Prop A does not change the Board's own appointments or the Police, Ethics or Elections commissions.
resp: "Every link in the chain of command will now end with you."

n4.s: Opponents say commissions give residents a place to be heard and a check on departments, and ending or weakening them cuts both.
g: limit public forums for city decision-making, remove important checks and balances, weaken transparency
Our city commissions were fought for by generations of activists.
still removes some important bodies for public participation
throws away the baby with the bathwater
Ultimately, Prop A reduces the independent oversight that keeps City Hall accountable to the public.
src: "These proposed changes would weaken civilian oversight, reduce transparency, and limit meaningful community engagement."
"Without the PWC, millions of dollars of construction contracts annually would be approved by the DPW Director, with no public visibility."
n4.fig: The two commissions Prop A ends were still meeting, though the streets one less often. The Public Works Commission met 23 times in 2023 and 11 times in 2026 through September 24. The Sanitation and Streets Commission met 4 times in 2025, including a joint budget hearing and a special meeting, after adopting a thinner 2025 calendar unanimously on November 18, 2024 with no reason given. The task force staff memo that warned of "no public visibility" went on to say bid protests give losing bidders "adequate recourse" and that citywide reforms made "one of the PWC's core reasons for being less relevant". SPUR, which supports Prop A, says ending bodies "may modestly reduce" public access.
resp: "For example, the Sanitation and Streets Commission oversees a department that doesn't exist"

n5.s: Opponents say the long package hides consequential changes, from a clash with June's term limits to looser rules on utility bonds, under a cleanup label.
g: trying to hide something in the fine print
src: "No person having served two successive four-year terms may serve as a supervisor, either by election or appointment, until at least four years after the expiration of the second successive term in office."
"Proposition A does not impact or make any changes to term limits"
n5.fig: Several changes appear in no official summary. Prop A reprints as unchanged the term-limit sentence June's Prop B struck. It deletes the Board's power to review SFMTA stop sign and bike lane decisions, which was never used for either. It removes the two-thirds Board vote, referendum clause and 30-day wait on one of three routes for PUC revenue bonds; 24 recorded Board votes on those bonds since 2009 all had at least 10 yes votes, and no referendum was found. It deletes the rule letting surplus utility revenue go to the General Fund with a unanimous PUC and 9 supervisors; none has moved since 2002 (the last was $29.85 million in 2000), and state law (Prop 218) bars diverting water and sewer fee revenue. It rewrites the Board's vote rule so only the Charter, state law, a voter ordinance amending itself, or Board rules can require more than a majority. Open question: which controls on term limits, November's Prop A or June's Prop B? The only official word is the City Attorney's office telling Mission Local Prop A "does not impact or make any changes to term limits"; there is no written opinion or ruling. Open question: which supermajorities do the new §2.104(b) and §4.104(b) vote rules end? A search found two set by past Boards, a 9-vote rule for the Emergency Reserve Fund and an 8-vote rule for the Hetch Hetchy completion finding; for commissions only Charter thresholds would remain. Open question: does deleting the surplus rule and the bond referendum change anything in practice for power revenue, which Prop 218 doesn't cover? No official reading exists.
resp: "nearly all are technical, administrative, or housekeeping changes"

n6.s: Opponents say fixed qualifications for seats on bodies like the Sunshine Ordinance Task Force become suggestions, opening seats to political appointees.
g: turns required commissioner qualifications into optional suggestions
it would let the board gut the independence of the sunshine ordinance task force
City Supervisors won't be bound to specific qualifications when making appointments, but should take them "into account." Political patronage appointments cronyism will mushroom!
src: "the Board of Supervisors is not bound to specific criteria in appointing members to the Task Force, but should take into account the following desired qualifications"
"Making these qualifications desirable, but not mandatory, runs the risk that viewpoints essential to deciding cases may be unrepresented or underrepresented in the future."
n6.fig: The change covers seven Sunshine Ordinance Task Force seats, the Public Utilities Commission's five seats (one labor seat stays required) and the Homelessness Oversight Commission's seats, where two stay reserved for people who have experienced homelessness. The Society of Professional Journalists' and League of Women Voters' nominations to the Sunshine task force stay. The Civil Grand Jury found 20% of advisory body seats and 11% of decision-making seats vacant in 2024, but three Sunshine task force members wrote in December 2025 that it "has had little difficulty in filling seats". The Sunshine task force didn't meet from June to October 2026 because of a holdover rule in Ordinance 99-26, a separate law. The paid argument's claim that a former Mandelman campaign staffer and a former Lurie aide seek Sunshine seats was not checked. Unverified.
resp: "Update language to mitigate legal risk and comply with State Law"

n7.s: Opponents say Prop A drops commissions' annual reports and loosens audit and performance reporting, so the public sees less.
g: it lets most commissions stop publishing annual reports
some would reduce community oversight and reporting requirements
"Prop. A" removes the requirement Boards and Commissions prepare annual reports, eliminating transparency for San Franciscans and City Supervisors!
src: "each board and commission of the City and County shall be required by ordinance to prepare an annual report describing its activeties"
n7.fig: Prop A deletes the Charter's annual report rule for commissions, a rule the Charter itself left for the Board to set by ordinance; whether a separate ordinance still requires reports was not found. The street, sidewalk and park audit drops from yearly to once every five years. The City has already cut back: "In total, FY26 included 735 evaluations on 368 routes," and the program "reduced the number of evaluations due to budget constraints"; DataSF's street evaluation data has none for FY2012-13 or from July 2018 to December 2021. Required benchmark reports are deleted; the last citywide benchmarking report found is dated February 16, 2017. SFMTA's duty to update a climate plan every two years goes; its last found update was approved March 21, 2023 and says the agency "previously did a major update in 2017". No later SFMTA climate plan was found by web search, and a June 2024 Vision Zero benchmarking item was not retrieved. Unverified.
resp: "multiple departments being required to create the same report, forcing employees into busy work that wastes time and money."

n8.s: Opponents say a standing task force with power to enact its own ordinances, plus commissions moved into code, make further cuts easier later.
g: makes it easier in the future to further reduce City Hall's transparency.
not making it easier to dismantle
making it easier for them to dismantle essential commissions
src: "Such ordinance(s) shall be deemed enacted 90 days after the date of introduction unless before the expiration of the 90-day period two-thirds of all members of the Board of Supervisors vote to disapprove the ordinance."
"I am also concerned by the pattern of proposals that fail to gain public support but continue to return until voter fatigue sets in, and they eventually pass."
n8.fig: The current task force already has this enact-unless-vetoed power; Prop A makes it come back every ten years from 2035 and drops the cost report and draft Charter amendment that went with it. It cannot reach bodies only voters can change. The 12 sections moved to code can later be amended by a Board majority, and the Board may rename any department or body by ordinance, including names in the Charter.
resp: "These are arguments for thoughtful and responsible implementation of Prop A, not for preserving an outdated charter."

n9.s: Opponents say bundling about 110 changes into one yes or no vote leaves voters unable to accept some and reject others.
g: combines many consequential changes in a single measure and would weaken or make it easier to change several channels for public oversight.
nothing good comes from pouring everything and the kitchen sink into the meatgrinder
Prop A would make 100+ changes to the City's charter and overhaul the city commission structure.
The Task Force developed an anti-democratic, 166-page Trumpian "Project 2025"-style commission reform Charter Amendment
src: "San Franciscans have no way of knowing how the proposed language in this particular Charter Amendment will interact with Mayor Lurie's other three Charter Amendments"
"They aren't "government streamlining efficiencies." They're SPUR's "Charter for Change"!"
n9.fig: The measure revises 79 Charter sections, deletes 14 and adds two, across 34 printed pages of legal text. A 2008 appeals court decision, as the San Diego City Attorney reads it, holds that the single-subject rule doesn't apply to charter amendments a governing body places on the ballot. No statement was found on why the changes went into one measure. The City Attorney's first draft of the task force's full plan runs 167 pages in the March 2026 packet, 166 without the cover. The case itself was not opened, and whether a court would apply that reading here was not tested. Unverified.
resp: "A voter reading the digest could reasonably conclude that this measure is primarily about commissions and advisory bodies, when in fact that category represents well under half of its total scope."

n10.s: Opponents say wealthy donors behind the Mayor's agenda are funding Prop A, along with his measures D, E and F.
g: They all go along with each other, no matter how bad the idea is, as long as Trump's billionaires benefit.
supported by $8 million in billionaire tech money
Billionaires sought "Proposition A" after losing 2024's Board and Commission reform "Proposition D" ballot measure to "Proposition E."
src: "Our current city government as represented by our elected officials is primarily monolithic, representing monied and corporate interests"
n10.fig: Yes on A raised $452,505 and reported $406,550.25 in expenditures through October 28, $400,826.25 of it paid; four donors gave $350,000, or 77%: Michael Moritz $150,000, Christian Larsen $100,000, Robert Fisher $50,000 and William Oberndorf $50,000. No committee formed to oppose it. Its largest payees were Cornerstone $175,352.78 (mail, including $107,186.33 in postage), Viewpoint $85,000 and Allbee $45,000 (consultant). GrowSF reported $18,433.83 and SPUR $5,822.64 in independent spending for it. The Mayor's committee for D, E and F reports $13,790,128.94, about 30 times Yes on A. The Bay Guardian's $8 million wasn't traced to a filing, and the Ethics dashboard says "This site is under development - accurate figures are not represented." Unverified.
resp: "Prop A is a good government housekeeping measure that cleans up and modernizes San Francisco's lengthy, outdated charter to serve you better."

y1: Prop A deletes the Sanitation and Streets and Public Works commissions, requires an ordinance ending the Advisory Committee of Street Artists and Crafts Examiners, and folds two aging and Dignity Fund advisory groups into one council. The meeting counts come from the Public Works Commission video archive and the Sanitation and Streets calendar, and the task force report counts 152 bodies and 1,560 meetings staffed in FY2024.
y2: New §18.116 says its "sole purpose" is to move these sections and "enable these sections to be amended or deleted in the future" like other Board-adopted law. The task force's examples of outdated Charter bodies include "The Special Strike Committee no longer complies with State law", and Mission Local reported the $117,000 figure for the 2024 campaign.
y3: The budget denominator is the FY2026-27 total in DataSF, the $33,894,772 and the per-body costs come from the analyst's survey of 111 bodies, and the 8% is the Civil Grand Jury's interview estimate. Payroll data show two Public Works executive secretaries costing $320,498 in FY2024-25 and $345,565 in FY2025-26, near the Controller's $336,000, though the data don't say which unit they serve.
y4: The City Attorney's digest groups many of these as "General Clean-up and Modernizing Amendments" consistent with the intent of current Charter language. Prop A also deletes the rule that contract laborers be U.S. citizens and obsolete 1996 transition sections, and the payroll check covered every Law Library job title from FY2012-13 to FY2025-26.
y5: Administrative Code §6.3(b)(1) has the Mayor approve awards for departments under the Mayor, and §3.3(b)(2) sets the department-run budget meeting for departments with no commission; Charter §10.104 says department heads serve "at the pleasure of the appointing authority". The task force staff memo said the commission's review "adds at least six weeks to the department's contract execution".
y6: The City's page says "The Shelter Monitoring Committee was eliminated effective June 29, 2026", and the task force wrote that "five bodies advise the City on homelessness". The crosswalk row on the Our City Our Home committee is the only stated reason found in the file and hearings.
y7: The Controller says each future task force "would require staff to implement and administer the CSTF, including conducting analyses, writing public reports, and holding public meetings". Its report goes to the Mayor and Board in early 2036 and gets a Board hearing by April 1 of that year.
y8: The sponsor said the changes came from departments, the task force and a Charter reform working group, in three groups: cleanup, department "PAIN POINTS" and task force bodies. The proponents' argument is signed by the Mayor, eight supervisors, State Senator Wiener and Assemblymembers Stefani and Haney; the rebuttal to the opponents by Mandelman and Lurie alone.
n1: The six required changes end the street artists' advisory committee, loosen Sunshine Ordinance Task Force qualifications, recodify the refuse ordinance, rename two oversight bodies and drop a Historic Preservation step for legacy businesses. Charter §14.100 extends referendum to "acts or measures involving legislative matters", and §14.102's procedure is worded for ordinances.
n2: The fund and committee figures are from the Controller's FY25 annual report and the street counts from the City's 2024 and 2026 point-in-time releases; the 5,000 and 1,700 are from the Coalition's December 2025 letter. Member Walton asked for a committee discussion of the task force's recommendation on October 23, 2025 and January 22, 2026; it was never scheduled.
n3: Administrative Code §6.3(b)(1) has the Mayor approve contract awards for departments under the Mayor, and Charter §10.104 says department heads serve "at the pleasure of the appointing authority". The Board's rejection route for mayoral appointments, §3.100(18), is reprinted in the Prop F legal text, and the Board's index of votes lists 8 votes to reject.
n4: The meeting counts come from the Public Works Commission video archive and the Sanitation and Streets calendar and minutes, and vacancies on either commission were not rechecked for 2026. The Sanitation and Streets chair wrote in September 2025 hoping its work would be seen "not as an area to scale back, but as an opportunity to strengthen oversight and standards".
n5: The bond vote counts come from every §8B.124 ordinance found in Legistar since 2009, the stop sign review rests on Ordinance 127-18, and the supermajority examples come from the Board's own index of votes required. June's Prop B passed with 53%, per Mission Local, which also quotes the sponsor saying the reprint "was absolutely not my intention".
n6: The Sunshine Ordinance Task Force discussed the measure on June 3, 2026 and took "No action". The Civil Grand Jury's vacancy rates are citywide, and the Homelessness Oversight Commission's appointing authorities "shall consider" the listed experience and diversity for all seats.
n7: The street figures are quoted from the Controller's FY26 report; DataSF says its evaluation data "cannot be used to calculate a citywide average". Prop A also drops each commission's annual statement of purpose and its required executive secretary.
n8: Commissioner Andary asked supervisors to reject the task force change because it no longer requires the analyst's report or a City Attorney draft. The Board's renaming power is new text in §4.100, and the current task force's power to enact ordinances is in §4.100.1 today.
n9: The single-subject reading is from the San Diego City Attorney's memo on Hernandez v. County of Los Angeles (2008), and the 167 pages are Attachment B of the March 16, 2026 Civil Service Commission packet. Prop A's own Section 2 sets rules for reading it together with D, E and F if more than one passes.
n10: The committee figures are from its Form 460 through October 28 and the Ethics dashboard; payments of $30,000 to Bedford Grove and $17,000 to Marrow carry no code or description in the data. GrowSF's own cumulative figure on its Form 496 is $18,433.83, while its four itemized rows sum to $18,139.71.
